ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Synergy as a signature of genuine computation
ideas.statement: When a target neuron's activity depends on the joint pattern of its inputs in a way that cannot be recovered from any single input alone, that irreducible joint information is treated as evidence the target is combining and transforming its inputs into something new, not just relaying them.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Densely interconnected hub neurons are the network's computational core
ideas.statement: Because rich-club neurons are unusually densely interconnected and carry a disproportionate share of information flow, they are treated as the sites where the circuit does its heaviest computational work, not merely as busy relay points.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: An inferred statistical network stands in for real circuit wiring
ideas.statement: A set of statistically significant directed dependencies (transfer-entropy edges) between recorded units is treated as tracing the actual pathways along which information travels in the underlying biological circuit, rather than as a purely correlational summary of the recordings.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Undirected correlation versus directed flow as different questions
ideas.statement: A measure of shared statistical dependence between two variables answers a different question than a measure of how one variable's past uniquely shapes another's future beyond what the second variable's own history already explains; the first is functional similarity, the second is directed influence.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Joint information need not equal the sum of individual contributions
ideas.statement: The total information that a group of sources jointly carries about a target can be greater or less than the sum of what each source carries on its own, revealing hidden synergy or redundancy that is invisible if sources are examined one at a time.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Redundancy has no unique definition within classical information theory
ideas.statement: The equations relating total joint information to redundant, unique, and synergistic pieces are underdetermined; ordinary Shannon theory supplies the joint and marginal mutual informations but leaves the split among redundancy, uniqueness, and synergy unfixed, so an extra measure or assumption must be introduced to pin it down.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: The number of decomposition components explodes combinatorially with source count
ideas.statement: The number of distinct redundant, unique, and synergistic pieces produced when decomposing information from k sources grows according to the Dedekind numbers, a sequence that increases so fast that a complete decomposition becomes computationally and practically unmanageable once there are more than a handful of sources.

ideas.label: I8
ideas.name: A partial order over source-combinations plus Möbius inversion yields a unique decomposition
ideas.statement: Once a redundancy function is fixed, all possible non-redundant combinations of sources can be arranged in a lattice ordered by which combinations subsume which others, and applying Möbius inversion over that lattice assigns a single well-defined value to every distinct mode of information sharing, exhaustively accounting for the total.

ideas.label: I9
ideas.name: Synergy peaks at intermediate, not maximal, input similarity
ideas.statement: As two input sources feeding a common target become more statistically similar to each other, the synergistic information they jointly provide about the target first rises with that similarity but then falls once the sources become too redundant, so the greatest joint computation happens at an intermediate rather than a maximal level of input correlation.

ideas.label: I10
ideas.name: Information measures can be defined event-by-event, not just as averages
ideas.statement: Rather than reporting only the expected (dataset-averaged) amount of shared information, an information quantity can instead be computed separately for every individual observed configuration of the variables, producing a value that changes at every moment in time rather than one summary number.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Knowledge from large-scale pre-training transfers to small downstream tasks via fine-tuning
ideas.statement: A model trained on a large, broad dataset can have its learned parameters adjusted on a much smaller, specific dataset, and the result will retain and apply what was learned at scale to the smaller task.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: A frozen representation's linear-fit accuracy indicates its underlying quality
ideas.statement: If you freeze a model's internal representation and see how well a simple linear classifier fitted on top of it can predict labels, that score reflects how good the representation itself is, independent of further training.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Performance keeps climbing with scale, without leveling off
ideas.statement: As models and datasets are made larger, accuracy keeps improving rather than flattening out at some ceiling, which is itself evidence that further investment in scale is still worthwhile.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: An image can be processed as a sequence of patch tokens
ideas.statement: Instead of feeding an image to a network pixel by pixel or through sliding convolutional filters, an image can be cut into small square patches, each patch flattened into a vector, and the whole image then treated as an ordered list of these vectors—exactly the way a sentence is treated as an ordered list of word vectors.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Data scale can replace built-in structural assumptions
ideas.statement: A model with no special assumptions about geometry or locality can still learn to handle that geometry, as long as it sees enough examples; the usual built-in assumptions (like a convolutional network's locality and translation invariance) mainly act as a shortcut for small datasets, not a requirement for good performance.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Pixel-level attention is too costly, so attention must operate on larger units
ideas.statement: Letting every pixel attend to every other pixel scales with the square of the number of pixels, which becomes computationally impossible for ordinary image sizes, so any workable image-attention scheme has to attend over a much smaller number of larger units instead of raw pixels.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: Spatial layout can be learned rather than hard-coded into position markers
ideas.statement: Rather than designing position markers that explicitly encode row, column, or distance in a 2D grid, a model can be given plain, unordered position labels and left to work out on its own, from the data, which labels correspond to nearby or far-apart locations.

ideas.label: I8
ideas.name: Compare models by performance achieved per unit of training cost, not performance alone
ideas.statement: When judging whether one model design is better than another, the relevant comparison is not just final accuracy but accuracy relative to how much computation it took to reach it.

ideas.label: I9
ideas.name: Average attention span works like a receptive field
ideas.statement: How far, on average, a given attention head reaches across the image when deciding what to combine can be measured and treated as the attention-based counterpart of a convolutional network's receptive field size.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Physical after-effects as stand-ins for direct measurement
ideas.statement: When a transient event cannot be measured directly, the marks, residues, or timed sounds it leaves behind can be treated as reliable stand-ins for measuring its physical properties, such as speed, energy, or composition.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Professional training upgrades eyewitness reliability
ideas.statement: A person's scientific or professional training is presented as making their account of a strange, brief event more trustworthy and more scientifically usable than an ordinary bystander's account.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Popular imagery can outlive and distort the documented facts
ideas.statement: A dramatic story or picture about a phenomenon can take hold in public imagination and persist as its defining image even after the factual record shows something more mundane.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Ball lightning may be several different phenomena
ideas.statement: The seemingly contradictory reports of ball lightning may not describe one single physical process but several distinct types or mechanisms lumped under one name.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Isolated, uncoordinated research fragments a field
ideas.statement: When data collection, theorizing, and laboratory testing on a phenomenon proceed separately without coordination, the result is a scattered, inconclusive body of research rather than a converging science.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Independent lightning-detection data can corroborate testimony
ideas.statement: Matching an eyewitness account's time and place against automated lightning-location network records provides an independent check on an otherwise unverifiable personal report.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: Elite samples reveal reporting biases when compared to mass data
ideas.statement: Comparing a small set of expert-observer reports against a much larger general public database can expose how the type of observer shapes which characteristics of an event get noticed and recorded.

ideas.label: I8
ideas.name: Shock trauma splits into separate immediate and lasting effects
ideas.statement: A sudden physical shock can produce two distinct kinds of harm that must be diagnosed separately: a short-lived direct physiological disruption and a separate, longer-lasting psychological disorder.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: A result only counts if it could have come out otherwise
ideas.statement: An experiment or comparison only demonstrates something scientifically if it was genuinely capable of turning out differently, and if the same test can be repeated to check that it does turn out the same way again.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: A shrinking effect under better controls was never real
ideas.statement: If an experimental effect gets weaker and weaker as the methods used to detect it are tightened and its flaws are removed, that pattern itself shows the effect was an artifact rather than a real phenomenon that merely needed better proof.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Cargo Cult Science copies form, not substance
ideas.statement: A field can reproduce every outward step and ritual of scientific work — controls, formulas, publications — and still fail to produce real results, because it is missing the one ingredient that actually makes the method work.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Integrity means volunteering evidence against yourself
ideas.statement: Being honest as a scientist is not just refusing to state falsehoods; it means actively disclosing facts, alternative explanations, and doubts that could weaken your own claim, even when no one is asking for them.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: You must catch your own self-deception first
ideas.statement: The primary discipline in science is guarding against fooling yourself, since you are more easily deceived by your own hopes and expectations than any outside critic could deceive you; honesty toward others follows only after that.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Posture as a window onto a hidden cognitive mode
ideas.statement: An animal's outward posture, such as standing up on its hind legs, can be treated as a reliable external signal of a distinct internal mode of attention or information processing, precise enough in time to target with a machine.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Disrupting encoding, not retrieval, is enough to erase a memory later
ideas.statement: Silencing the hippocampus only while information is first being taken in, and leaving it untouched when the animal is later asked to recall that information, is assumed to be sufficient to show a memory deficit, because the critical hippocampal contribution is located at the moment of taking in information rather than at the moment of recalling it.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Hippocampal importance varies by behavioral state
ideas.statement: The hippocampus does not contribute equally to memory at all times; its role depends on what the animal is doing moment to moment, so some behavioral periods (like moving or resting) may matter for memory formation while others may not.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Elevated theta during rearing as rationale for its memory relevance
ideas.statement: Because rhythmic hippocampal theta activity is known to support encoding and retrieval, and rearing is accompanied by a boosted form of theta, rearing was suspected in advance to be a period when memory-relevant hippocampal processing occurs.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Two error counts separate what was forgotten from how well errors were corrected
ideas.statement: Counting whether the first four choices are correct measures whether the animal remembers which arms it already emptied, while counting the total number of arms visited measures a different thing: how efficiently the animal corrects course after a mistake, so the two numbers track separate memory demands.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Timing, not total dose, of disruption determines its effect
ideas.statement: Whether silencing the hippocampus impairs memory depends on whether the silencing is precisely aligned with the behavior of interest, not merely on how much total disruption occurs during the study period.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: Rearing updates a spatial map against the pull of yesterday's memories
ideas.statement: Active upright sampling of the environment may let an animal revise its mental model of where rewards currently are, specifically by separating today's trial-specific facts from the interfering memory of many nearly identical past trials.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: A single-cell-line mouse tumor model stands in for diverse patient tumors
ideas.statement: Findings from a xenograft grown from one human breast-cancer cell line in mice are treated as representative of the general molecular process by which real, genetically varied patient tumors become resistant to tamoxifen.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Co-rising markers across tumors are read as mechanistically linked
ideas.statement: If two molecular markers tend to rise and fall together across a group of different tumors, that statistical pattern is taken as evidence that the two signaling pathways are mechanistically connected inside each tumor's cells, not merely that both happen to be present together.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Tumors can switch their dominant growth driver over time
ideas.statement: As a cancer is treated and progresses, the molecular pathway actually driving its growth can change, so a tumor that depended on estrogen signaling at diagnosis may come to depend on a different signal by the time it resists treatment.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: ER signals both from the nucleus and from the cell membrane
ideas.statement: Besides its classic role of entering the nucleus and switching genes on or off, the estrogen receptor also acts at the cell membrane to rapidly trigger growth-factor signaling cascades, and those same cascades can loop back to activate the receptor.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Kinase phosphorylation can turn tamoxifen from blocker into activator
ideas.statement: When growth-factor or stress kinases such as those downstream of HER-2, p38 and ERK add phosphate groups to the estrogen receptor and its helper protein AIB1, they can switch the tamoxifen-bound receptor into an active state, so the drug ends up mimicking estrogen's growth-promoting effect instead of blocking it.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: True identities must hold necessarily, so apparent contingency needs explaining away
ideas.statement: If two expressions genuinely name the very same thing, their identity cannot be a mere accident that could have failed to hold; it must be necessary, so whenever a proposed identity feels like it could have been otherwise, that feeling is something to be explained rather than treated as evidence the identity is false.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Experience is defined by "what it is like"
ideas.statement: An organism counts as conscious exactly when there is something it is like to be that organism from the inside; this subjective quality, not any particular behavior or capacity, is what consciousness fundamentally is.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Function and behavior can be faked without experience
ideas.statement: Describing a mind entirely through its functional organization or its causal role in producing behavior does not rule out the possibility of a being that fits the description perfectly while feeling nothing at all, so such descriptions cannot be the whole story about mental states.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Unconceivable facts can still be real
ideas.statement: There can be genuine facts - such as what it is like to be a bat - that exist and are true even though no human being will ever be able to form the concepts needed to state, picture, or fully grasp them.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Experiential facts belong to a type of viewpoint
ideas.statement: Facts about what an experience is like are tied to a particular kind of vantage point; they can be grasped by anyone similar enough to share that vantage point, but understanding them gets harder, not just more detailed, as a creature's point of view diverges further from one's own.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Objectivity moves reduction away from experience, not toward it
ideas.statement: Ordinary scientific reduction gets more accurate by stripping away any one species' or individual's viewpoint and describing things in terms accessible from many perspectives; applying that same strategy to experience does not bring us closer to its true nature, because experience just is a specific viewpoint, so shedding the viewpoint loses the very thing being explained.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: Saying "X is Y" explains nothing without a bridging framework
ideas.statement: An identity claim like "mental states are physical states" only becomes understandable once there is some theoretical picture of how the two descriptions could pick out the same thing; the word "is" by itself conveys no such picture and can disguise an empty claim as an explanation.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Skull form reliably reveals inner character
ideas.statement: The shape and proportion of a person's head can be read to accurately disclose the strength of their underlying mental faculties, without need for further behavioral evidence.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Harmony of faculties, not raw strength, is what matters
ideas.statement: Success and virtue come from the faculties working together in balance; a powerful faculty left uncoordinated with the rest produces failure or vice rather than advantage.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Marital happiness depends on matching combinations of faculties
ideas.statement: Compatibility between partners is a matter of which faculties and temperaments each possesses, and a marriage fails or succeeds according to whether these combinations suit each other, independent of wealth or appearance.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Innate organization fixes the ceiling of what a person can become
ideas.statement: A person can improve and even excel within their natural sphere, but effort and desire cannot carry them past the limits set by their inborn mental and physical organization.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Reading a child's organization early allows pre-emptive correction
ideas.statement: Because a child's dominant faculties can be identified before they fully manifest in behavior, a parent or teacher can intervene in advance to prevent an excessive faculty from ever becoming a problem, rather than reacting after the fact.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Mental states can cause and cure bodily illness
ideas.statement: The mind acts on the body directly, so that disappointment, grief, or a strong will can produce genuine physical prostration or resist medical treatment, and a change of mental state can restore health.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: The same faculty is virtue or vice depending on degree and control
ideas.statement: No mental faculty is bad in itself; the identical trait that drives success when exercised proportionately becomes crime or disease when it is excessive, deficient, or unchecked by the moral faculties.

ideas.label: I8
ideas.name: Guilt should be measured against a person's given moral equipment
ideas.statement: Two people who commit the same act are not equally guilty; the one whose organization gave them more capacity for restraint and better moral faculties bears greater responsibility than one whose organization left them poorly equipped to resist.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Reputation enforces behavior in a small, repeated market
ideas.statement: Because founders and investors will keep running into each other and because word travels in a small community, each side's future opportunities depend on how they behaved in past dealings, which disciplines behavior more than any contract does.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Only costly commitments carry information
ideas.statement: Spoken interest or encouraging words cost an investor nothing to give and nothing to retract, so they tell you nothing; only an action that would be costly to reverse (a signed offer, wired money) reveals what someone actually intends.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Leverage comes from alternatives, not neediness
ideas.statement: A founder's bargaining power in a deal depends on having other options or the ability to walk away, not on how much they are liked or how hard they try to please the other side.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Investors are caught between fear of missing out and fear of a flop
ideas.statement: Investors want to wait for more certainty before committing, but waiting risks losing the deal to a competitor, so this tension produces herky-jerky, misleading, often slow behavior rather than clean yes-or-no answers.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Fundraising is an attention-consuming state, not a time cost
ideas.statement: Fundraising harms a company less by the hours it takes than by occupying a founder's mind so fully that everything else, especially the daily work that grows the company, stalls; so a startup should be cleanly in fundraising mode or cleanly out of it.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Search investors in parallel, weighted by expected value
ideas.statement: Talk to all prospective investors at once rather than one at a time, but give more time and attention to the ones whose probability of saying yes times the value of their check is highest.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: A first commitment triggers a cascade of other commitments
ideas.statement: Once one investor commits money, other investors' willingness to invest rises sharply because their own judgment of a startup is heavily driven by what other investors think, making the very first yes disproportionately hard to get and disproportionately valuable once gotten.

ideas.label: I8
ideas.name: Needing money and not needing it are two different games
ideas.statement: Raising money while the company could survive without it (because it is near profitable) is a fundamentally easier and more pleasant process than raising money because the company will die or lay people off without it; these are different activities that happen to look similar from outside.

ideas.label: I9
ideas.name: Valuation is a distant third priority in fundraising
ideas.statement: What actually matters from a fundraise is getting enough money and getting good investors; the price at which you sell equity is a much less important number that founders tend to overweight because it is the only visible score.

ideas.label: I10
ideas.name: Take the best offer now rather than gambling on a better one later
ideas.statement: Because the future is unpredictable and because finishing fundraising quickly matters more than optimizing it, a founder should accept any sufficiently good offer immediately rather than holding out in hopes something better appears.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Calling something a lie presumes a fixed truth it departs from
ideas.statement: Labeling a belief given to children as a 'lie' only makes sense if there is some actual state of the world, independent of culture or consensus, that the belief fails to match.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Childhood lies leave a debt to be cleared later
ideas.statement: People reach adulthood carrying a backlog of falsehoods absorbed in childhood, and because no one later sits them down to list what was false, clearing this backlog out of one's own head takes deliberate, self-directed effort.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: A culture's lies to children form one seamless, agreed-upon conspiracy
ideas.statement: Adults within a culture quietly coordinate on the same set of falsehoods for children, so that the fabricated picture of the world has few visible seams and is usually discovered only through internal contradictions rather than direct exposure.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: A sheltered upbringing can leave adults naive about the real world
ideas.statement: Raising children in an artificially safe, sanitized environment protects them in the short run, but if that shelter is not corrected for later, it leaves them with an inaccurate, overconfident picture of how the world actually works.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Keeping children innocent keeps them able to keep learning
ideas.statement: Some kinds of knowledge, once acquired, make a person stop bothering to learn more; shielding children from cynical truths about the world preserves the open-mindedness needed for continued learning.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Group identity sticks because its beliefs are arbitrary
ideas.statement: Telling a child they belong to an ethnic or religious group works especially well as a lasting identity because the group's distinguishing beliefs and customs are arbitrary and false, and the resulting dissonance between holding them and being treated as an outsider pushes the child to claim the identity as their own.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: Calming lies to children breed adult complacency
ideas.statement: Lies told mainly to stop a child's distress, rather than to inform them, train people to feel that alarming realities are normal, which later makes adults complacent about problems that genuinely deserve urgency.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Nature versus nurture separated by twin and adoption comparison
ideas.statement: The relative contributions of heredity and environment to a trait can be teased apart by comparing people who share ancestry but differ in upbringing, or who share upbringing but differ in ancestry.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Eugenics as deliberate improvement of human stock
ideas.statement: Human populations can and should be improved across generations by deliberately encouraging reproduction among those judged to have superior inherited qualities and discouraging it among others.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Regression toward the mean
ideas.statement: Offspring or later measurements of an extreme trait tend to lie closer to the population average than the original extreme value did, not because of any corrective force but simply because extreme values are rare and most cases cluster near the middle.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Hard heredity: traits pass down unaltered by experience
ideas.statement: Inherited traits are carried by fixed hereditary material that selection can act on across generations, but which is not reshaped by what an individual does or experiences in its lifetime.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Simple sensory and motor measures as windows onto mental ability
ideas.statement: Performance on basic sensory discrimination and reaction speed can stand in for a person's general mental capacity, so measuring the body's responses is a way of measuring the mind.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Correlation as a measurable relationship between variables
ideas.statement: Two measurable traits can be linked by correlation: variation in one is accompanied, on average, by variation of a predictable size and direction in the other, without one necessarily causing the other.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: Socially important personality traits get encoded into language
ideas.statement: The personality differences that matter most to people living together tend, over time, to accumulate their own words, so sampling a language's vocabulary can reveal a map of the personality traits a culture tracks.

ideas.label: I8
ideas.name: Averaging many independent judgments approaches the truth
ideas.statement: When many people make independent estimates of an unknown quantity, their aggregate (the middle or average value) tends to be far more accurate than most individual guesses.

ideas.label: I9
ideas.name: A blended composite image can represent an ideal type
ideas.statement: Superimposing many individual photographs into one blended image was thought to cancel out individual quirks and reveal a generalized, idealized version of a category of person.

ideas.label: I10
ideas.name: Races as fixed, unequally ranked in inherited capacity
ideas.statement: Human racial groups were held to possess distinct and stable inborn levels of civilizational and intellectual capacity, with some races ranked permanently below others.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Long shots are worth it when the payoff is huge
ideas.statement: An attempt's worth is its chance of success times the size of the payoff. A small chance at an enormous gain can beat a sure modest one, and when single outcomes can't be predicted, making many attempts is the way to collect the rare big win.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Greedy choices can strand you on a local peak
ideas.statement: A greedy method always takes whichever next step looks best right now. Such a method can get stuck on a local maximum: a spot better than everything nearby but worse than the best spot overall, which could only be reached by first passing through something that looks worse.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: A successful discovery stops surprising later readers
ideas.statement: Because an essay works by teaching, its value depends on what readers do not yet know. When its ideas win and become common knowledge, the essay keeps its importance but loses its surprise. So lasting, evergreen appeal requires ideas that never fully sink in.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Questions need inspiration; answers yield to persistence
ideas.statement: Answers can be ground out by rewriting until they are right, so effort covers them. Good questions come from inspiration, often from curiosity about some odd small puzzle, and in the best work this supply of questions is what limits quality.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Writing turns vague ideas into fixable wrong ones
ideas.statement: Committing to specific words makes a hazy thought concrete enough to see where it is broken. Strict rereading then exposes gaps between the draft and the truth, and those gaps often point to new ideas or hidden false assumptions.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Children absorb attitudes toward work by watching adults, not by being told
ideas.statement: Kids come to feel that work is drudgery mainly by observing the emotional relationship the adults around them actually have with their jobs, rather than by anything those adults explicitly say.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Real enjoyment must show up as an admirable, checkable result
ideas.statement: Genuinely loving an activity isn't just a private feeling; it has to leave behind something you or others can point to and call impressive, or it doesn't count as evidence of real enjoyment.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Loving work has an upper and lower bound
ideas.statement: Doing what you love doesn't mean wanting to do it more than anything else at every single moment; it means, over a stretch of time like a week or month, preferring it to any idle pleasure and being able to point to something admirable that came of it.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Prestige warps perceived preference
ideas.statement: Prestige works like a magnet on judgment: it doesn't just reward existing achievement, it actively distorts what people believe they enjoy, pulling the ambitious toward work that merely looks impressive rather than work they'd actually choose.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: The unpaid-work test for genuine love
ideas.statement: The clearest way to check whether someone truly loves their work is to ask whether they'd still do it if they weren't paid for it and had to take another job just to get by.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: High-stakes evaluations get gamed rather than satisfied
ideas.statement: Once passing some evaluation becomes the thing that matters (getting into college, getting a good grade), people and institutions will work to satisfy the evaluators themselves rather than to achieve whatever the evaluation was originally meant to measure.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Belief in innate genius excuses laziness
ideas.statement: People who achieved great things were not a separate breed with magic innate talent; biographies make them look that way in hindsight, and believing in that magic gives ordinary people an excuse not to try as hard.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Keep options open instead of fixing a goal
ideas.statement: Rather than picking a distant goal and working backward from it, you should choose among present options the one that leaves you with the widest range of good choices later, and let the eventual goal emerge from that process.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: School substitutes fake tasks for real achievement
ideas.statement: Grades, discipline, and most extracurricular activities are proxy tasks that feel like accomplishment but are not the same as actually learning to do something hard and real, such as writing well or programming.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Real aptitude is narrow deep curiosity, not discipline
ideas.statement: What looks like talent or diligence in people who do great work is usually an intense, specific curiosity about some question, and that curiosity is what turns demanding work into something that feels like play rather than effort.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Big questions congeal from small self-chosen projects
ideas.statement: You cannot find a great question by searching for one directly; instead, great questions gradually form in your mind as a byproduct of spending real time on small, interesting, self-chosen projects, each one leading to the next.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Past startups' unscalable tactics generalize into advice
ideas.statement: Stories of what specific famous startups did early on (Airbnb's door-to-door recruiting, Facebook's Harvard-only launch, Meraki and Pebble building their own hardware, Stripe's manual merchant accounts) can be turned into reliable, transferable advice for a new founder, rather than being read as incidental details of companies that happened to succeed for other reasons.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Startups must be hand-started, not launched
ideas.statement: A startup rarely takes off by itself; it takes a deliberate, effortful push from the founders to get growth moving, after which it can sustain itself.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Tiny weekly gains compound into huge numbers
ideas.statement: Because a steady percentage growth rate multiplies on itself week after week, a small early user base that looks unimpressive can become enormous within one or two years if the rate is sustained.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: A young startup's fragility makes it easy to misjudge
ideas.statement: In their earliest weeks or months, startups are so fragile that a short burst of neglect or a short burst of effort can decide whether they live or die, which means judging them by the standards used for established companies gives the wrong answer.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: How you start can become permanently who you are
ideas.statement: The unscalable things founders do to get going are not just a temporary trick to escape afterward; they can imprint habits and values that stay with the company as it grows large.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Shared bone structure, not looks, reveals true kinship
ideas.statement: Two animals can look nothing alike on the outside yet be close relatives, and close relatives can look superficially similar to unrelated species; the real test of kinship is shared structural detail in the skeleton (and later, genes), not overall appearance.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Genetic divergence timing plus land age can date lost abilities
ideas.statement: Comparing how long ago two lineages' DNA split (estimated from mutation accumulation) against the known geological age of the land they live on can reveal facts about ancestors nobody observed, such as whether they could still fly.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: A copy of an image is not a second witness
ideas.statement: When a later picture is traced or adapted from an earlier one rather than drawn from life, it cannot be used as independent confirmation of what it shows; it only repeats the first image's errors.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: A reused name can make an extinct animal seem to linger
ideas.statement: If people start applying an extinct species' name to a different, still-living animal because they expect to see it, later records using that name do not prove the original species survived.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Flightlessness evolves where islands remove predators and competitors
ideas.statement: On islands without ground predators or competing mammals, flighted ancestors can lose the ability to fly and grow unusually large, because flight's main benefits (escape and competition) stop paying for its costs.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Captive or badly kept specimens distort how a wild animal looked
ideas.statement: Animals kept in captivity are commonly overfed or otherwise altered, and preserved specimens decay or get mounted oddly, so pictures and measurements based on them can give a false sense of what the species looked like in the wild.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: Where bones happen to settle skews what we can know
ideas.statement: The bones that survive and get found in one burial site are not a random sample of a population; currents, scavenging, and chance can leave some body parts and life stages overrepresented and others missing entirely, biasing later conclusions.

ideas.label: I8
ideas.name: Losing one species can collapse another's lifecycle
ideas.statement: An animal and a plant can become so mutually dependent during their shared evolution that the extinction of the animal breaks a step the plant needs to reproduce, and no newly introduced species does the job in quite the same way.

ideas.label: I9
ideas.name: Introduced animals, not hunting, usually doom island species
ideas.statement: On islands where humans are few, the deciding blow to a native species is typically not direct killing by people but the predators, competitors, and habitat loss that people bring with them.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Findings in one species can transfer to humans because the underlying biology is shared
ideas.statement: Studying a developmental or regenerative process in a distantly related animal is useful for understanding human biology because the molecular and structural machinery involved (heart chamber formation, neural tube closure, limb patterning) is conserved across vertebrates.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Scarring and regeneration are competing healing strategies
ideas.statement: An organism's wound can heal in one of two incompatible ways: fast closure by scar tissue, or slow rebuilding of the original structure, and suppressing the first (especially the inflammation that drives scarring) is what makes the second possible.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Neoteny is a broken hormonal switch, not a separate life stage
ideas.statement: Staying aquatic and sexually mature at the same time is not a special axolotl body plan but the result of a missing hormonal signal: without thyroid-stimulating hormone triggering thyroxine production, the change into a land-adult body never fires, so the larval body keeps reproducing.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Neoteny can be an adaptation, not just a leftover quirk
ideas.statement: Permanently remaining in the aquatic larval form can be favored by evolution when the water habitat is safe and the equivalent land habitat is risky or unsuitable, making neoteny a strategy rather than a developmental failure.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Population bottlenecks erode genetic diversity and long-term fitness
ideas.statement: When a population's numbers crash sharply, the survivors carry only a fraction of the original genetic variation, which increases inbreeding, raises the frequency of harmful mutations, and leaves the population less able to adapt or recover.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: A small founding stock reshapes a captive population's genetics
ideas.statement: When a whole captive or domesticated population descends from a handful of founding individuals, later generations can drift genetically and be reshaped by artificial selection, ending up noticeably different from their wild ancestors even while looking similar.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Group statistics can't diagnose one face
ideas.statement: A correlation found across a large population of faces says nothing certain about any single person's actual character; reading one individual's face as a sign of their nature is a different, stronger claim than reporting a statistical tendency across thousands of faces.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Doctrine of signatures applied to the face
ideas.statement: Nature was believed to mark its hidden properties visibly on the surface of things, so that the outward form of a plant or a face was itself a key, or 'signature,' to inward qualities a person could learn to read.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Criminality as an evolutionary throwback
ideas.statement: Lombroso's theory held that some people are 'born criminals' because they are biological throwbacks to an earlier, more primitive stage of human evolution, and that this ancestral nature shows up as specific inherited physical traits.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Perceived face shapes the behavior it claims to predict
ideas.statement: People treat others according to how their faces make them seem, and being treated that way over time can push a person toward actually behaving as expected, so a correlation between a face and a trait can be partly manufactured by other people's reactions rather than read off some fixed inner nature.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: AI face-reading often detects context, not structure
ideas.statement: When an algorithm appears to predict a trait from a face, the accuracy may come from incidental cues in the image—makeup, lighting, image quality, background—rather than from the facial structure physiognomy claims to interpret.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: A trait shaped by environment cannot mark a fixed race
ideas.statement: If a physical measurement like head shape can change because of environmental conditions rather than being passed down unchanged, it cannot serve as reliable evidence of a fixed, inherited racial category.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Numerical precision was used to dress up bias as objectivity
ideas.statement: Presenting a claim as an exact measurement in degrees, cubic inches, or cubic centimeters made a hierarchy of races or species look like a neutral scientific finding rather than an interpretive judgment.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Craniometry differs from phrenology and physiognomy
ideas.statement: Measuring the skull's physical dimensions (craniometry) is a separate enterprise from claiming that skull or facial shape reveals personality, character, or criminal tendency (phrenology and physiognomy), even though the same tools and techniques were later borrowed by the latter.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Reanalysis of old data is itself repeatedly contested
ideas.statement: Claims about whether a historical scientist's data was biased are not settled once and for all; each generation's reanalysis of the same skull measurements has been challenged by a later reanalysis.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Make the strongest claim that stays true
ideas.statement: Being exact and being correct pull against each other: a vague claim is safe but empty, and an overly sharp one is bold but false. Good writing pushes a claim as far as it will go without becoming false, and uses hedges such as "I think" or "perhaps" as a fine-grained dial for how sure you are, how widely it applies, and how you know it.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Usefulness is a product of four qualities
ideas.statement: A piece of writing is useful to the degree that it is true, important, new to many readers, and stated as strongly as possible. Each of these comes in degrees, and they multiply rather than add, so a near-zero in any one sinks the whole.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: For essays, publishing only your successes is right
ideas.statement: In science, reporting only the results that worked out (publication bias) distorts the record. For an essayist, though, quietly throwing away every sentence, passage or whole essay that does not hold up is the way to make sure everything published is good. You admit your mistakes before publishing rather than after.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Popular false beliefs hide unexplored ideas
ideas.statement: A widely held but mistaken belief creates a dead zone, a ring of nearby ideas that people avoid because those ideas contradict it. That makes such beliefs a good place to look for new ideas, and also explains why those ideas are met with anger rather than thanks.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Discomfort with idleness is trustworthy evidence you should work
ideas.statement: Feelings like restlessness, disgust at wasted time, or fear of failure are treated as reliable indicators that you are not doing real or sufficient work, and as legitimate forces to let drive your effort.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: Talent and effort are complements, not substitutes
ideas.statement: Doing the best possible work requires natural ability, practice, and effort all together; having great talent without great effort (or vice versa) only gets you partway there.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Real achievement requires wanting to work without being told
ideas.statement: Working hard toward goals set by someone else (as in school) is relatively easy even for children; the harder and more essential skill is generating the drive to work when no one is imposing the goal or the deadline.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Each person has a shifting daily ceiling on productive effort
ideas.statement: Beyond a certain number of hours, which varies by person and by type of work, pushing harder makes the output worse rather than better, so the right amount of work is a limit to be discovered rather than simply maximized.

ideas.label: I1
ideas.name: Ancestry correlation does not validate race as a natural kind
ideas.statement: Finding that genetic ancestry patterns statistically line up with some traditional racial labels does not establish that those labels pick out real, discrete, essential biological types; a continuous, many-dimensional pattern of ancestry is a different thing from a social act of sorting people into a fixed set of categories.

ideas.label: I2
ideas.name: A true clade requires shared exclusive ancestry, not just similarity
ideas.statement: In evolutionary biology, a group only counts as a genuine natural lineage (a clade) if it contains all and only the descendants of one common ancestor; populations can look similar or cluster together statistically without meeting this stricter requirement.

ideas.label: I3
ideas.name: Race is a social construct with real effects
ideas.statement: Race is not a fact of biology but an identity that societies create and assign based on perceived physical traits and ancestry, and although it lacks a biological basis, it still produces real consequences in people's lives through discrimination and institutional treatment.

ideas.label: I4
ideas.name: Colonial science invented ranked racial types
ideas.statement: The idea of race as a fixed, global, natural division of humanity was produced during European colonial expansion and Enlightenment natural science, which sorted human groups into a hierarchy that placed Europeans at the top and used this ranking to justify slavery and conquest.

ideas.label: I5
ideas.name: Human variation is clinal, not sharply bounded
ideas.statement: Physical and genetic traits such as skin color change gradually across geographic distance, with no natural breakpoint separating one group from the next, so continuous gradients (clines) describe human variation better than discrete racial zones.

ideas.label: I6
ideas.name: Most variation is within groups, yet individuals can still be sorted
ideas.statement: The bulk of human genetic variation occurs within any single population rather than between populations, and this fact can coexist with the ability to assign individuals correctly to their population of origin when enough genetic markers are used.

ideas.label: I7
ideas.name: Genetic clusters depend on which groups you sample
ideas.statement: The number and shape of genetic 'clusters' that emerge from population data are not fixed facts about nature but artifacts of which populations a researcher chooses to compare; sampling different populations produces entirely different clusters.

ideas.label: I8
ideas.name: Scientific consensus on race is itself historically variable
ideas.statement: How strongly scientists reject biological race, and whether they use the concept at all, has differed by country, discipline, and era, showing that the scientific treatment of race has its own social and historical pattern rather than being a single fixed verdict.

stops.paragraph: Our evidence supports the latter interpretation: post-training gains on SWE-bench do not consistently transfer to other code tasks, even within the same repository. To illustrate this, we build a Django benchmark covering code editing, generation, and completion, and evaluate community-released checkpoints and our fine-tuned models. We observe a consistent pattern across both community-released SWE-bench-oriented checkpoints and models we fine-tune. Models fine-tuned on issue-resolution trajectories do not generally improve on our Django-related tasks or LiveCodeBench (LCB) (Jain et al., 2024), while models fine-tuned on one of the Django tasks do not improve on other Django tasks or LCB. This suggests narrow training recipes drive task-specific specialization, not general coding improvement. Moreover, SWE-bench (and even multi-benchmark) rankings may not always reliably predict relative performance on these modalities. Together, our findings suggest that SWE-bench rankings may systematically misrepresent models’ relative strengths on individual SE tasks, particularly since real-world usage extends beyond agentic issue resolution.

stops.paragraph: In this position paper, we argue that this mismatch between performance on different benchmarks reflects a construct validity problem: when a small number of benchmarks is treated as a proxy for “general coding capability,” the resulting claims exceed what the measurements can actually support. SWE-bench targets a complex but specific behavior that involves navigating repositories, understanding issue descriptions, and producing targeted patches. These measurements may mix multiple underlying capabilities with narrow task-specific skills. High performance may indicate strong coding ability, but may equally reflect proficiency at the particular format and workflow developed under benchmark optimization pressure. Without evaluation across diverse task modalities, we cannot distinguish among these hypotheses, understand the strengths and weaknesses of our post-training approaches, or even assess the foundation models with sufficient granularity. The resulting misnterpretation can then spread to engineers and users working with LLMs and agents, as LLM-assisted coding and coding agents become increasingly common, and, in the end, undermine their trust in these systems.

stops.paragraph: The PID framework has a number of limitations that potentially complicate its application in naturalistic settings. The most significant is the explosive growth of the PI lattice. For a system with k parent neurons, the number of distinct PI atoms is given by the kth Dedekind number (minus two) [30]. This sequence of numbers grows appallingly fast: in the case of six parent neurons, there are 7,828,354 distinct PI atoms, the vast majority of which are difficult to interpret. Dedekind numbers greater than nine are currently unknown. Given that single neurons can receive inputs from very large numbers of upstream neurons, a “complete” description of the information dynamics of any individual neuron is completely intractable. This issue may be partially addressed by the development of heuristic measures of redundancy and synergy such as the O-information [65], which has been applied to information dynamics in networks of neurons [66] and human functional magnetic resonance imaging blood-oxygen-level-dependent (fMRI-BOLD) signals [67], although these measures typically trade completeness for scalability.
stops.cue: Note how many distinct components arise once there are six parent neurons to decompose.

stops.before: The original PID framework allows for the decomposition of the information that an arbitrary set of parents provides about a single target. A natural generalization is to allow for multiple targets. For example, what synergistic information about two targets is disclosed by the synergistic joint state of two parents? In the context of a temporally evolving process, the same analysis could be used to decompose the redundant, unique, and synergistic ways that the past constrains the future. A recent multi-target generalization of the PID, termed integrated information decomposition (ΦID) [69,70] has been proposed, which opens the door to a much wider range of possible analyses than is possible with a single-target PID analysis. ΦID analysis of fMRI data has found changes in the flow of synergistic information associated with loss of consciousness [46,71] and the genetic architecture of the brain [44]. A recently introduced “temporal redundancy function” (Iτsx), coupled with a ΦID analysis, led to the discovery of a set of sixteen distinct information dynamics associated with the temporal evolution of pairs of interacting neurons, many of which were previously unknown [45]. Due to its comparative novelty, multi-target information decomposition has received less attention than its single-target counterpart, and consequently, a number of open questions remain.

stops.paragraph: In this paper, we have aimed to provide an accessible introduction to the partial information decomposition framework [1] and shown how it can be applied to answer fundamental questions about information processing in neural circuits. We have focused particularly on statistical synergy, i.e., the information about the future of a target neuron that is disclosed by the higher-order patterns instantiated by multiple upstream neurons and is irreducible to any single source, as a measure of processing or computation. The existence of synergy in empirical data shows us that neurons do not appear to blindly sum the number of inputs and fire in response to the total (as would be expected from a basic threshold model or complex contagion model), but instead they are also sensitive to the particular patterns of incoming stimuli. Furthermore, not only does the existence of statistical synergy add nuance and dimensions to our understanding of the dynamics of individual neurons, we have also shown that the patterns of synergistic information processing are informed by the local environment in which those neurons are embedded (rich club membership, motifs, clustering, etc.), as well as the behavioral state of the oganism under study. These findings hint at the existence of a large, potentially fruitful space of future research relating higher-order information dynamics to biological, cognitive, systemic phenomena at many scales of analysis.

stops.before: Naive application of self-attention to images would require that each pixel attends to every other pixel. With quadratic cost in the number of pixels, this does not scale to realistic input sizes. Thus, to apply Transformers in the context of image processing, several approximations have been tried in the past. Parmar et al. (2018) applied the self-attention only in local neighborhoods for each query pixel instead of globally. Such local multi-head dot-product self attention blocks can completely replace convolutions (Hu et al., 2019; Ramachandran et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2020). In a different line of work, Sparse Transformers (Child et al., 2019) employ scalable approximations to global self-attention in order to be applicable to images. An alternative way to scale attention is to apply it in blocks of varying sizes (Weissenborn et al., 2019), in the extreme case only along individual axes (Ho et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020a). Many of these specialized attention architectures demonstrate promising results on computer vision tasks, but require complex engineering to be implemented efficiently on hardware accelerators.

This was also remarked by Thottapillil (2005, p. 31) in his COST Action proposal P18 on the physics of lightning together with 30 European researchers and the consensus that “the reality of ball lightning is not in doubt.” Rakov and Uman (2003, p. 656, p. 658) characterized ball lightning as “a phenomenon for which there exists numerous witness reports but little, if any, scientific documentation such as photographs, videotapes, or other scientific recordings.” They counted almost 5000 observation reports. “There may be more than one type of ball lightning and more than one mechanism by which ball lightning is generated”, they continue, also “There have been many theories devised to explain ball lightning. None is completely satisfactory” and “many luminous phenomena created in the laboratory are claimed by their creators to be ball lightning”. For the same reason, Turner called ball lightning research a “fragmented science” (2001).
stops.cue: Notice what this expert verdict says is missing from most reports of ball lightning.

stops.before: “Guarda! Guarda!” (“See! See!”) – calls from the Corsa dei Servi (central street, now Corso Vittorio Emanuele II) in the centre of Milan alarmed Lorenzo Butti, marine painter of the Empress of Austria. It was 18:00 LT (local time) in June 1841, with a heavy thunderstorm outside. Butti looked out of the window where people were running in the rain under a reddish-yellow ball of fire. It travelled at window height of the second floor, rose higher, and then exploded at a church tower cross with a dull crash. The artist wrote his experience to physicist Arago. Arago’s report was rediscovered by senior school official Walther Brand for his monograph “Der Kugelblitz” (1923, 2010), the only one in German to date.

stops.paragraph: Since Sur le tonnerre of French astronomer and physicist François Arago (1837), the term ball lightning (Kugelblitz, foudre globulaire) stands for a still unexplained group of metastable luminous phenomena in atmospheric electricity. Ball lightning appears seemingly random in time and space, lasts a few seconds, and disappears with traces or without. Because of its unpredictable occurrence, most of the collected material remains anecdotal.
stops.cue: Notice what the unpredictable timing of these sightings means for the kind of evidence that gets collected.

stops.paragraph: Chances to monitor the transient phenomenon directly are minimal: Tompkins et al. (1975) searched about 12 000 photographic records of the US Prairie Meteorite Network that observed the night sky daily for over 10 years and found two probable ball lightning events. Other photographic or video records (e.g. 1935 Berlin; 1976 Transvaal, South Africa; 1978 Montafon, Austria; 1985 Lake Undugun, Russia; or 2003 Zwönitz, Germany) were also random products. Therefore, Singer (1971, chap. 5.B.2) and Stenhoff (1999, chap. 10.4) paid special attention to ball lightning reports coming from scientists or trained professionals. However, large databanks like Rayle’s (1966; N = 112 reports) and McNally’s (1966; N = 513 reports) from the US did not ask for observer’s professions and degrees. Published ball lightning reports of scientists are scattered, and even more remain unpublished.
stops.cue: Notice how rare a direct photographic capture of the phenomenon turns out to be.

The time of 2 s for 100 m was faster than the free fall which would have taken about 5 s.

stops.paragraph: Walther Gerlach, physics professor at the University of Tübingen, wrote a report to Naturwissenschaften on 20 May 1927: “On 9 May 1927, 08:00 [LT] I observed ball lightning [at Tübingen] . . . I happened to stand at the window . . . In the northeast, linear lightning went down with strong ramifications. From it (apparently out of a sharp kink) came a bright luminous yellowish-white ball in a considerable height and flew to the southwest. The time between lightning and the ball’s flyover of our institute was roughly 1 s. It could be observed for another second in the same appearance on its straight trajectory, soundless. Two seconds later, a not very strong thunder started, and 1.5 s after its start, there was an extraordinarily violent detonation, like an explosion bang.” Gerlach did his calculations: with a speed of sound of 330 m s−1 and observed times of the lightning’s thunder and the explosion, he got a ball lightning trajectory of 1300 + 1150 = 2450 m. In 2 s flight time, “ball lightning had a mean speed of about 1200 m s−1”. “I learnt at noon that the ball hit a small, barn-like house on the edge of Tübingen which is 1100 m distant . . . the top of an electrical mast was smashed nearby.” Gerlach also mentioned bluish “spraying” of electrical wires and blown fuses in “a whole row of houses” (Gerlach, 1927). His speed calculation of 1225 m s−1 is quite amazing, because it means the object travelled at a speed of Mach 3.6 “soundless”, without an acoustic effect (sonic boom). This is one of the rare occasions where ball lightning met a gifted experimental physicist. Gerlach is renowned for his 1922 experiment about spin quantization in a magnetic field.
stops.cue: Notice what everyday trace, left behind by the event, was used to work out this extraordinary speed.

stops.before: The author, meteorologist and psychologist, collected, evaluated, and published European ball lightning cases for 45 years (Keul, 1980, 1981, 1992, 1993, 1994, 2004; Keul and Stummer, 2002; Kugelblitz, 2021). For most of this period of time, ball lightning case work was limited to single case investigations and statistical synopses, lacking an interdisciplinary perspective with forensic experts, materials science, lightning protection experts, etc. The upswing of modern lightning location networks (like BLIDS, German lightning information service, or ALDIS, Austrian lightning detection and information system) opened up new options, so recently, a first correlation of 34 central European ball lightning events, 1994–2016, with lightning location data was done together with ALDIS (Keul and Diendorfer, 2018). Nineteen detected strokes, correlated in time with ball lightning, were positive (4–370 kA peak current) and 15 were negative (−3 to −37 kA). Twenty-eight were cloud–ground strokes and 6 were cloud–cloud strokes; 28 occurred in the summer months and 6 in winter. Seventeen events had close-distance lightning strokes – ball lightning under 1 km (mean 0.42 km), and 17 were distant events (1–10 km, mean 5.7 km). The unexpectedly high number of positive strokes and the equal frequency of close and distant events were discussed at the 34th International Conference on Lightning Protection.

stops.paragraph: We start our series of cases with a chronology of eyewitness reports by natural scientists, and technical and medical experts. Several alleged observations (e.g. of Niels Bohr and Victor Weisskopf), often quoted in science or popular journals, were incorrect or lacked data: Tuck (1971) only wrote that he heard from Weisskopf that Bohr had once seen ball lightning. Martin Ryle was quoted without details by Davies (1987). Pyotr Leonidovich Kapitsa developed a ball lightning theory but reported no alleged sighting. Geologist and mineralogist Wilhelm von Haidinger, member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences at Vienna, observed ball lightning from his home at Vienna’s 3rd district Landstrasse on 20 October 1868, in a heavy thunderstorm between 17:15 and 17:30 LT: “The electric fireball was one of the very first discharges of the thunderstorm . . . It stood maybe 2–3 s in front of the right pane of the window . . . It is indeed simple to describe the ball, of a vivid yellow light, especially on the right . . . while on the left . . . clearly red, with longer rays than the ball, firing from it to the right and towards the earth, of red, yellow colour, up to the most dazzling white. Also, left there were shorter rays inclined obliquely towards the earth. . . . Several discharges followed and after [them] hail and rain.” Haidinger (see his sketch in Fig. 1) determined the object’s angular diameter as 0.83°. After his observation at Ungargasse 3, 3rd district, to the southwest, Haidinger heard about other occurrences in Vienna. Four of them sound like ordinary lightning but two described ball lightning: P. Joseph Dobner, Haidinger’s friend, took shelter from the thunderstorm in a friend’s home at Magdalenenstr. 32, 6th district. He saw a glaring blue sphere outside the window to the southeast. stops.before: The German graduate physicist Hans Dolezalek, working on atmospheric electricity after 1961 for the US Navy, reported his own observation at Tübingen, Baden-Württemberg, Germany (Dolezalek, 1951). On 8 June 1951, about 17:00 LT, a thunderstorm started. Minutes before 18:00 LT, Dolezalek saw ball lightning like a car headlight 30 m away, moving downwards aslant with about 50–100 m s−1, disappear behind trees. A violent bang was heard, like an explosion or a grenade launcher, followed by a rising blue smoke cloud. The object’s impact with 10 m bright rays spreading upwards was seen by another observer in a meadow. Later, a 50 cm burned spot was found. Two isolators of a 5 kV power line pylon 5 m from the impact point were damaged. Neckar power station Hirschau (connected to the 5 kV line) registered an interruption at 17:54 LT.

stops.paragraph: Coroner Leopold Breitenecker, later a forensic medicine professor at Vienna University, encountered ball lightning at Ternitz, Lower Austria, in the summer of 1955, 16–17:00 LT. He carried out an autopsy with a colleague in an old mortuary during a heavy thunderstorm, when lightning struck and threw the electricity meter out of the wall. From the hole in the wall, a fist-sized, sharply outlined ball descended to the floor, radiating a bluish white light like a welding arc. It moved 5 cm above the floor to the open door but disappeared into the stone wall beneath the door frame. The witness threw down his instruments and leapt to the door just in time to see the ball (apparently after passing through a crack in the wall) move across the vestibule and out of the mortuary’s front door. It bounced down the steps like a toy ball and disappeared into a grave mound after travelling 8–10 m in about 5 s (Keul, 1980, 1981). Breitenecker saw ball lightning a second time from Mühlbach/Attersee, Upper Austria, in the summer of 1975, late afternoon, looking towards Mt Schafberg in a thunderstorm with many lightning flashes. Suddenly, a distant fireball travelled horizontally along a mountain wall, then burst sparking, like a spray candle.
stops.cue: Notice this witness's later profession, and how precisely he placed the time and location.

stops.paragraph: A citation classic in ball lightning literature (Singer, 1971; Barry, 1980) as well as in popular articles is the case of Georg Wilhelm Richmann, a Baltic German physicist and member of the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences, who, during work on atmospheric electricity, was electrocuted in 1753. From an investigation protocol with autopsy results (Anonymous, 1755, pp. 64–68), it is obvious that it was a conventional lightning accident caused by a non-grounded conductor. However, a popular engraving pictured a lightning ball that hit Richmann. As in the 1818 Frankenstein novel, the grim fate of an avantgarde scientist sounded plausible. Ball lightning acquired a deadly and destructive popular image fed by injuries and damage caused by ordinary cloud–ground strokes.
stops.cue: Ask what kind of ordinary event is being blamed for ball lightning's fearsome reputation.

stops.before: On 23 June 2008, at about 20:45 LT, Rozlyn Krjcik, administrative director emeritus of the New York State Spinal Cord Injury Center, Poughquag, New York, USA, arrived at her Poughquag home by car in heavy rain and with lightning around. I saw that fiery ball, yellow-flame appearance in my front door. . . . It was the centre of the door, at least twice, two and a half times more area than you’d expect from that small cantaloupe-size blue object I saw.” The glowing blue sphere was 14 cm in diameter and then flew away between her house and her car. Calibrated quantitative fluorometry measurements of the NY porch window in June 2016 found that for a floodlight illumination, the object’s ionizing-radiation output was 10 W; if considerably brighter, it was 100 W.

stops.paragraph: An innovative field experiment was carried out by Martin A. Uman’s US research group (Hill et al., 2010): at the military base Camp Blanding, Florida, the group had already triggered numerous lightning strikes by rockets with a trailed metal wire. In 2008, triggered lightning was conducted to over 100 substances on the ground, including salt water, silicon wafers, stainless steel, or conifer branches. The resulting phenomena were photographed and analysed. So, a flame was created for over half a second over salt water, glowing silicon fragments fell down for 1 s, a flashover on the steel surface formed a 33 cm ball of light, and the discharge into the conifer branches was visible for half a second. Uman and colleagues call what was produced not ball lightning but point to interesting effects of different materials under the influence of lightning.
stops.cue: Notice what these researchers concluded their lab-made effect actually was, and was not.

stops.before: The main difference between modern science and Frankenstein’s laboratory is guiding research paradigms that – in the case of natural phenomena – condition a proper order of systematic data acquisition, formation, and testing of hypotheses and theories, and – if possible – laboratory simulation. In the case of ball lightning, the research logic is distorted by a random phenomenon that is hard to observe, irreproducible, and mostly reported by change. Weird popular press stories and a lack of economic (except some military) interest did not encourage scientific community nor weather services to deal with this “unsolved problem in atmospheric physics” (Stenhoff, 1999). Most ball lightning research was (and still is) part-time and individualized – some people collecting data, some theorizing, some doing laboratory tests. Big databases (e.g. Brand, Stakhanov, Rayle, McNally) ended and amateurs took over, theorists opened at least 16 explanatory domains (Rakov and Uman, 2003, p. 664), and a diversity of laboratory simulations developed laterally.

stops.paragraph: I think the educational and psychological studies I mentioned are examples of what I would like to call Cargo Cult Science. In the South Seas there is a Cargo Cult of people. During the war they saw airplanes land with lots of good materials, and they want the same thing to happen now. So they’ve arranged to make things like runways, to put fires along the sides of the runways, to make a wooden hut for a man to sit in, with two wooden pieces on his head like headphones and bars of bamboo sticking out like antennas—he’s the controller—and they wait for the airplanes to land. They’re doing everything right. The form is perfect. It looks exactly the way it looked before. But it doesn’t work. No airplanes land. So I call these things Cargo Cult Science, because they follow all the apparent precepts and forms of scientific investigation, but they’re missing something essential, because the planes don’t land.
stops.cue: What name does the speaker give to science that copies every outward ritual but still fails to get real results?

stops.before: Now it behooves me, of course, to tell you what they’re missing. But it would he just about as difficult to explain to the South Sea Islanders how they have to arrange things so that they get some wealth in their system. It is not something simple like telling them how to improve the shapes of the earphones. But there is one feature I notice that is generally missing in Cargo Cult Science. That is the idea that we all hope you have learned in studying science in school—we never explicitly say what this is, but just hope that you catch on by all the examples of scientific investigation. It is interesting, therefore, to bring it out now and speak of it explicitly. It’s a kind of scientific integrity, a principle of scientific thought that corresponds to a kind of utter honesty—a kind of leaning over backwards. For example, if you’re doing an experiment, you should report everything that you think might make it invalid—not only what you think is right about it: other causes that could possibly explain your results; and things you thought of that you’ve eliminated by some other experiment, and how they worked—to make sure the other fellow can tell they have been eliminated.
stops.quote: If you make a theory, for example, and advertise it, or put it out, then you must also put down all the facts that disagree with it, as well as those that agree with it.

stops.paragraph: Details that could throw doubt on your interpretation must be given, if you know them. You must do the best you can—if you know anything at all wrong, or possibly wrong—to explain it. If you make a theory, for example, and advertise it, or put it out, then you must also put down all the facts that disagree with it, as well as those that agree with it. There is also a more subtle problem. When you have put a lot of ideas together to make an elaborate theory, you want to make sure, when explaining what it fits, that those things it fits are not just the things that gave you the idea for the theory; but that the finished theory makes something else come out right, in addition.
stops.cue: Notice what a researcher is required to disclose about their own theory, not just what supports it.

stops.paragraph: These convergent reasons led us to hypothesize that rearing is an epoch of hippocampal dependent encoding of spatial memories. To test this hypothesis, we selectivity inactivated the dorsal hippocampus during rearing events in a spatial memory task. Hippocampal activity was manipulated with closed-loop, bilateral, optogenetic inactivation triggered by a 3D camera system calibrated to detect rearing. Manipulations of hippocampal activity were restricted to the study phase of an 8-arm maze delayed-win-shift task41,42. Behavioral assessments were performed during the subsequent test phase. We found that inactivation of the dorsal hippocampus during bouts of rearing resulted in impaired spatial memory at test. Hippocampal inactivation for matched amounts of time but delayed relative to rearing events, did not produce significant memory impairments. stops.before: Spatial memory requires an intact hippocampus. Hippocampal function during epochs of locomotion and quiet rest (e.g., grooming and reward consumption) has been the target of extensive study. However, during navigation rats frequently rear up onto their hind legs, and the importance of hippocampal activity during these periods of attentive sampling for spatial memory is unknown. To address this, we tested the necessity of dorsal hippocampal activity during rearing epochs in the study phase of a delayed win-shift task for memory performance in the subsequent test phase. Hippocampal activity was manipulated with closed-loop, bilateral, optogenetic inactivation. Spatial memory accuracy was significantly and selectively reduced when the dorsal hippocampus was inactivated during rearing epochs at encoding. These data show that hippocampal activity during periods of rearing can be important for spatial memory, revealing a novel link between hippocampal function during epochs of rearing and spatial memory.

stops.paragraph: The study protocol was approved by Indiana University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. All animal procedures and surgeries were conducted in accordance with the ARRIVE guidelines and in strict accordance with National Institutes of Health and the Indiana University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee guidelines. Adult (at least 3 months of age) Long Evans rats (sourced from Envigo Inc.) were used for all experiments. A total of 18 rats were used: 8 male rats were in the experimental group. 2 rats dropped due to failure to reach behavioral criterion. 10 rats (5 female; 5 male) were in the control group 1 female rat dropped due to failure of the surgical implant. 2 male rats dropped due to failure to reach behavioral criterion. 7 rats (4 female; 3 male) were used for analysis. Animals were individually housed and maintained on a 12 H light/dark cycle in a temperature and humidity-controlled room with ad libitum access to water and food restricted to maintain~90% (85–95%) of free feeding body weight. Rats were acclimated to the animal facility for 5 days before being handled daily. Due to the overt signaling of conditions via optogenetic manipulation and the timeline of the study, the experimental group data was collected first, followed by the control group. The experimenter could not be blinded to condition or group.

stops.before: The optogenetic experimental conditions were as follows: in the main experimental condition wherein light was delivered coincidentally with rearing behavior, referred to as ’Rear’ in the results, the laser was activated as the 3D camera system detected rearing and remained on for the full duration of the rear.
